blogs.title: The Perils of Contradictory Expertise: Why Self-Impeaching Testimony Cannot Support a Jury Verdict
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Federal Circuit's reversal regarding the '134 patent, focusing on the evidentiary standard for infringement when a plaintiff's sole expert offers contradictory testimony. The article will explore how Chief Judge Moore applied *Johns Hopkins Univ. v. Datascope Corp.* to determine that Dr. Wells' inability to consistently map claim limitations to the accused device's architecture rendered the evidence legally insufficient. It discusses the tension between the jury's role as fact-finder and the court's gatekeeping function when an expert's narrative collapses under cross-examination, signaling a stricter scrutiny of 'pivot' arguments made by experts to salvage infringement theories.

blogs.title: Prosecution History Estoppel and the 'Three Signals' Requirement: Distinguishing Disavowal from Clarification
blogs.description: Focusing on the '775 patent, this analysis examines the court's nuanced treatment of prosecution history estoppel. While the Federal Circuit rejected AT&T's argument that amending claims from 'two or three' to 'three' signals constituted a clear disavowal of two-signal systems, it simultaneously found no infringement based on the mathematical impossibility of performing the claimed seven multiplications with only two inputs. The post will dissect why the court distinguished between surrendering scope on the *number* of unique inputs versus the *mechanism* of multiplication, offering guidance on how patentees can amend claims to overcome prior art without inadvertently narrowing their coverage beyond intent.

blogs.title: Mapping Mathematical Claims to Reality: The Fatal Flaw in Equating Distinct Operations with Claimed Multiplications
blogs.description: This post dives into the technical and legal specifics of the '775 patent infringement analysis, specifically the requirement to perform seven distinct third-order multiplications. The article highlights the court's rejection of Finesse's attempt to map three distinct operations in the accused device (involving modulus and complex conjugates) onto seven claimed multiplications. It serves as a cautionary tale for litigants in software and signal processing cases: relying on post-hoc mappings not presented to the jury or failing to demonstrate how specific algebraic operations in an accused product align with every step of a highly specific method claim will result in JMOL being granted as a matter of law.
